results.title: A hybrid approach to record linkage using a combination of deterministic and probabilistic methodology
results.content: Deterministic linkage methods, when performed independently, yielded 4505 linked pairs (consisting of 2 records linked together within or across data sources). However, the fragmented US healthcare system and the nonexistence of a universal patient identifier across systems necessitates accurate record linkage (RL) solutions.1,2 Individual-level health data are often scattered across disparate healthcare systems, particularly for individuals with complex chronic conditions.3 Without a universal unique patient identifier, RL is accomplished using personally identifiable information (PII) such as first name, last name, date of birth, and social security number.4,5 However, variable patterns of data quality and missingness in PII between data sources may impact RL performance.6. More advanced deterministic methods enable approximate matching by comparing encoded data (eg, SOUNDEX) instead of original linkage variable values or fuzzy matching algorithms.9,10 Probabilistic methods are computationally more complex but perform well even in the presence of missing or erroneous RL data values.11,12 The most widely used probabilistic RL technique is the Fellegi–Sunter method which calculates the likelihood of a match/nonmatch outcome based on the weighted agreement of each linkage variable.13,14 Probabilistic methods generate a normalized continuous match score ranging from 0 (nothing in common) to 100 (all linkage variables match exactly). Preference for using deterministic versus probabilistic linkage methods depend largely on factors such as quality of linkage data (eg, presence of erroneous or missing data), performance priority (precision, recall, and F-measure), and linkage efficiency (runtime).11,12,15,16 Differences in linkage performance between the 2 methods diminish as the size of the data set increases, and if combined, allows researchers to leverage the advantages of each method.17 We describe the implementation and evaluation of a hybrid RL method that improved linkage accuracy in a statewide surveillance system of a rare chronic disease: the Colorado Congenital Heart Disease (COCHD) Surveillance System. Therefore, data normalization is typically performed on linkage variables such as first name, last name, date of birth, address, phone number, and social security number (SSN).19–25 Duplicate records will likely exist in each data source and will be detected in the final linkage results. In this population-based congenital heart disease surveillance system, we have shown that, when performing RL and de-duplication of individuals within and across disparate data sources, a hybrid RL routine outperformed independent deterministic and probabilistic linkage methods.

results.title: Probabilistic vs Deterministic linkage - Splink
results.content: There are two main types of record linkage - Deterministic and Probabilistic. Deterministic Linkage is a **rules-based** approach for joining records together. While Splink is primarily a tool for Probabilistic linkage, Deterministic linkage is also supported (utilising blocking rules). Probabilistic Linkage is a **evidence-based** approach for joining records together. In a large dataset, observing that two records match on the full name 'Robert Smith' provides some evidence that these two records may refer to the same person, but this evidence is inconclusive. Given these probabilities, unlike (binary) Deterministic linkage, the user can choose an **evidence threshold** for what they consider a match before creating a new unique identifier. Splink is primarily a tool for Probabilistic linkage, and implements the Fellegi-Sunter model - the most common probabilistic record linkage model.

results.content: The question, which variables to use for matching, usually arises in the probability matching stage. The suggested approach in this paper is to define sufficiently precise sets of variables already in the exact matching stage. Such sets of variables may be used for exact matching with little likelihood of mistake. Sequential use of exact matching by different sets of variables enables finding most of the correct matches in a short time even for large files. • By using SPSV the exact matching may be carried out quickly without the complicated procedures of examining record pairs and clerical review. • The information about which sets of variables and in what order we should use them is required anyway for probability matching. • The concept of RL using a Master File can help avoid some of the problems due to duplicates and the matching precision will make the RL more reliable in due course. These are inherent problems in probability matching, and it has been shown here that they can be solved in the exact matching stage as well. After exact matching is carried out, the record linkage is carried out by probabilistic methods. For our data, the index used for determining the matching status is calculated as a weighted sum of agreement indices for names, age and gender. The model is built for data sets that passed clerical review and had the true matching status for each record. The upper and lower thresholds for determining the different classes of the matching status are based on the classical Neyman-Pearson method for hypothesis testing. In 1969, Ivan Fellegi and Alan Sunter formalized a strategy for conducting probabilistic record linkage that had been developed previously. Included in this formalization was the demonstration that the scoring method used with this is optimal under certain assumptions. While other record linkage methods have been developed (including Bayesian-based ones) for large-scale linkages the Fellegi-Sunter approach should be a strong candidate.

This talk provides an overview of the Fellegi-Sunter approach, explaining how candidate pair are evaluated under it.
